chunks: Say: 'Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?' Say: 'God.' Say: 'Then why do you take protectors besides Him who have no power over their own gain or loss?' Say: 'Can a blind man and one who can see be equal? Or, darkness and light be the same? Or, have those they have appointed equal of God created, as He has created, so that the (two) creations look alike to them?' Say: 'God is the creator of everything. He is One, the omnipotent.'
ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?' in Surah Ar-Ra'd?
ai.summary: In Shia exegesis, this verse is often cited to refute the attribution of independent agency to saints or imams, clarifying that while they are 'awliya', they possess no power of benefit or harm except by God's permission. The rhetorical questions highlight the logical absurdity of associating partners with the Creator, reinforcing the concept of Tawhid al--Tafwid (Delegation of Authority) where divine power remains absolute. This passage serves as a foundational argument against polytheism by contrasting the active, all-powerful Creator with inert, powerless idols.
